transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in to see me?

My head keeps getting stuck on these awful what‑if scenarios about things going wrong with the wiring, and I can’t shut the thoughts off long enough to do my job. It's just really starting to take a toll on me.

Do these thoughts feel intrusive and repetitive in a way that you try to resist or neutralize with specific actions, like checking the wiring over and over, or do they feel more like general worry about many different things?

They are definitely intrusive, looping images of awful disasters like a house catching fire, rather than just general worries. To try and stop them, I end up checking the same outlet or panel five or ten times—tugging wires and flipping breakers—until I feel this "click" in my chest that says it's safe. If I don't do it just right, I have to start all over, which is completely derailing my work.
When you do the checking, do you feel driven to repeat it because of a fear that something terrible will happen unless it is done exactly right?

Yes, absolutely. I am terrified that a house will catch fire or someone will get electrocuted if I don't do it perfectly. I feel this intense drive to keep flipping breakers and tugging wires until I get that specific "click" in my chest, and if it doesn't feel exactly right, I have to start the whole sequence all over again.
About how much time each day do these thoughts and checking rituals take up, and are they interfering with work, sleep, or other daily activities?

They take up hours of my day, keeping me awake late at night and constantly delaying my work because I have to repeat checks five to ten times. It has gotten so bad that I've lost a major contract, had to turn down good jobs, and completely stopped going to softball and theater because I just can't relax or focus on anything else.
Do you mainly have repeated checking rituals, or do you also have other repetitive behaviors like washing, cleaning, ordering, counting, or mental rituals?

It's really just the checking rituals related to my electrical work, like flipping breakers, tugging wires, and re-reading the code book over and over. I don't have any washing or cleaning rituals, but I feel compelled to repeat these checks five or ten times until I get that "click" in my chest, or else I have to start the whole sequence over.
Do you ever have repeated thoughts or rituals about things other than checking electrical safety, such as cleaning, ordering, counting, or other kinds of checking?

No, I don't really experience any of those other rituals like cleaning, ordering, or counting. My focus is pretty much entirely on the electrical safety and checking the wiring over and over to make sure it's safe.
Do you recognize that these checking rituals are excessive or unreasonable, even though you feel unable to stop them?

Logically, I know it is completely excessive and doesn't make sense, especially since I tell myself the work has already passed inspection and is perfectly fine. But the anxiety and those looping images of disaster are so intense that I feel completely powerless to stop until I get that "click" of safety in my chest. It’s incredibly frustrating to know how unreasonable it is while it’s actively ruining my livelihood.
Do you also get unwanted intrusive thoughts or urges about contamination, symmetry, counting, or needing things to be arranged a certain way, or is it only the electrical safety checking?

No, it is really just about the electrical safety and the fear of someone getting hurt or a fire starting. I don't have any of those thoughts or urges about contamination, symmetry, or counting. While I've always been neat and meticulous with my wiring layouts for work, it's nothing like these obsessive safety checks.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has classic obsessive-compulsive symptoms dominated by intrusive, repetitive obsessional images of disaster and compulsive checking rituals focused on electrical safety. He recognizes the thoughts and rituals are excessive, but feels driven to repeat them to reduce anxiety and prevent feared harm. Symptoms consume hours daily and cause clear occupational and social impairment, with no evidence of another OCD subtype or a better alternative diagnosis.
